planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so propagation is vegetative.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. Debbie is an intergeneric Graptopetalum-Echeveria hybrid forming compact rosettes of thick, powdery, pastel pink to lavender-purple leaves that deepen toward magenta at the tips with strong sun and cool nights, a rich, saturated color that stands out among grayer or greener succulent companions. It offsets readily from the base to form a spreading clump over time, and detached leaves that fall cleanly will root and grow into new plants, making it easy to multiply. Trim any lengthening stems to keep rosettes low and compact, and repot every couple of years into fresh gritty mix.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Blue Elf Sedeveria (Compact Blue-Green Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so propagation is vegetative.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. Blue Elf is an intergeneric Sedum-Echeveria hybrid forming small, tight, blue-green rosettes with a light powdery bloom, blushing pink-orange at the leaf tips in strong sun and cool weather. Its compact, clumping, offsetting habit fills a small pot or the front of a mixed succulent bowl quickly without becoming leggy, and stray offsets can simply be pulled off and set on top of fresh mix to root and start new clumps. Water thoroughly then let the mix dry out completely before watering again, since overwatering is the most common cause of rot in this group of hybrids.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Little Jewel Pachyveria (Chalky Blue-White Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a hybrid it does not come true from seed, so propagation is vegetative.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. This intergeneric Pachyphytum-Echeveria hybrid, widely sold as Little Jewel, forms small, tight rosettes of thick, plump, egg-shaped leaves coated in a heavy chalky-white to pale blue-gray bloom that rubs off easily if handled, so it is best displayed where it will not be brushed against. The compact, slow-growing rosette offsets modestly at the base over time, and dropped leaves will readily root and grow into new plants if left undisturbed on top of the soil. Water thoroughly then let the mix dry out completely before watering again, since overwatering is the most common cause of rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun; Blue Chalksticks spreads by trailing, rooting stems and makes an excellent low groundcover in a xeriscape bed or container.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun, allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. Blue Chalksticks produces upright, finger-like, powdery blue-gray leaves along spreading, semi-woody stems that root as they trail, forming a dense, low, silvery-blue mat useful as a groundcover, container spiller, or texture contrast against green or purple succulent companions. Small clusters of white, faintly fragrant flowers appear occasionally but are secondary to the striking foliage color, which is at its bluest in full sun and lean soil. Trim back leggy stems to encourage denser branching, and avoid overwatering, since soggy soil is the most common cause of rot.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun; Blue Fingers grows more upright than the closely related Blue Chalksticks and makes a good structural accent in a xeriscape bed or container.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun, allowing the soil to dry fully between waterings. Blue Fingers is closely related to Blue Chalksticks but grows in a more upright, clumping form with longer, thicker, distinctly finger-shaped blue-gray leaves, giving it a bolder, more architectural presence useful as a mid-height accent in a mixed succulent planting rather than as a low groundcover. Occasional small white flowers appear but are secondary to the striking foliage color, which is at its bluest in full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Trim back leggy growth to encourage denser branching, and avoid overwatering, since soggy soil is the most common cause of rot.
